## Policy Reference

### 1. Task Breakdown & Lifecycle (`todowrite`)
- **Pre-edit Gate:** All file-editing tools (`edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`) are blocked while the session's effective todo list is known and contains no active task. On OpenCode 1.x the list comes from the native todo system (`todowrite`, persisted at `GET /session/:id/todo`). Before 2.1.0, the OpenCode 2.x builtin tool registry has no `todowrite`, and there is no todo endpoint. The list is then reconstructed from the newest applied `todowrite` tool call in the session history, which ACP agents may supply. OpenCode 2.1.x reintroduces a builtin `todowrite` behind the `experimental.todo` config key. The guard detects that capability by probing the host tool registry rather than inferring it from history. Verified on 2.1.3: `ctx.tool.list()` exposes `todowrite` when the flag is on, and omits it when off. The gate distinguishes a **definitively empty** list from an **undeterminable** one. A definitively empty list means the capability exists and reports no active task, which stays blocked. An undeterminable list means no todo capability, or the history cannot be read. The gate then fails open and records that once per session at warn level. This keeps builtin-only V2 sessions usable instead of deadlocking every edit forever.
- **Flexible Task Execution:** Tasks can be completed in any order as work concludes without artificial sequential blockers, maintaining maximum pair-programming DX.
- **No Silent Deletion:** Each `todowrite` update replaces the complete list. Active tasks must remain in subsequent updates until they are explicitly marked `completed` or `cancelled`.
  - **Refinement, not deletion:** An active task may be reworded when its replacement keeps every word of the original and adds at least one more. That is the same work item sharpened, so the write passes and the task keeps its original mutation window. Two distinct words is the floor, so a one-word task always needs an exact match. Each replacement absorbs at most one removed task. Every accepted refinement is journaled as `todo_refined`. A reword that drops or substitutes a word is still a removal and blocks.
- **Per-Task Completion Evidence (enforced):** Because a `todowrite` call replaces the whole list, a model can mark work `completed` without doing it. A task may therefore enter `completed` only when the session recorded at least one file mutation inside that task's active window. One mutation cannot vouch for several completions, so N completions require N mutations counted from the earliest of them. Mutations spent before a task became active never count toward it. A blocked write names the task and the remedy. The check also runs in simulation, so `guard_why` predicts the gate instead of reporting a falsely permissive verdict. A finished or dropped task releases its window, so reusing the same task text starts clean. Tasks are matched to their prior occurrences by count, so duplicate text cannot hide a new completion behind an already-completed item. The mutation counter records permitted mutation calls, not confirmed byte changes.
  - **Planned late:** a task first observed already `completed` has no window to judge, so it is scored against the session's mutation history instead. This is the deliberate path for an agent that did the work before writing the list. It stays bounded by the one-mutation-per-completion rule.
  - **Read-only escape:** A task whose text carries `[read-only]`, also `[read_only]` or `[read only]`, completes without a mutation. Review, investigation, and reading are legitimate work that changes no file. The marker is an annotation, not part of task identity, so it can be appended to an already-planned task without reading as a deletion. Every use is journaled as `todo_completed_read_only`, so relabeling real work as read-only stays visible in the audit trail. In a repository with no detectable verify command, that journal is the only counterweight. Work that was deliberately dropped uses `cancelled` instead.
  - `guard_status` reports `taskEvidence` (`active`, `completed`, `tasksWithoutRecordedWork`, `readOnlyTasks`), so the requirement is visible before it blocks anything. This is not task authority. Fresh verification evidence and the review gate remain the authority on finalization.
- **Todo Capability Visibility:** Because the gate depends on the host exposing `todowrite` at all, `guard_status` reports `todoCapability` (`available` / `unavailable` / `unknown`). A fail-open gate is therefore visible rather than decorative.
- **No Silent Early Exit:** When an owning session reaches the idle state with unfinished native todos, the guard asynchronously asks OpenCode to resume the existing run. That trigger is `session.status` with `status.type === "idle"` or the deprecated `session.idle`; both are in `EventManifest.ServerDefinitions`, and which one the server publishes is not settled, so neither is relied on alone. A host that emits both for one transition still produces a single continuation prompt, because the send holds a per-session in-flight lock. This enforces the session's existing lifecycle state. Workflow Guard does not choose the next task, reorder work, create work, or delegate it. Ordinary automatic continuations are capped at three consecutive attempts, and the budget resets on genuine user input. User-initiated interrupts (Esc) suspend automatic continuation for that session until genuine user input arrives, mirroring the ralph `user_stopped` semantics. On OpenCode 2 this is driven by `session.execution.interrupted`, and only reason `user` suspends: `shutdown`, `superseded`, and `inactivity` are host-lifecycle events, not user intent, and they leave continuation state alone. The independently opt-in `ralphMode` uses `ralphMaxIterations` (1-100, default 10) instead. Genuine user input terminates an active Ralph run, and unfinished work at the budget limit reports `budget_exhausted` rather than inferring a policy block. Ralph remains disabled by default under every operation profile. Use OpenCode's native `question` tool when user feedback or a decision is required. Question and permission interactions wait inside the active run rather than producing an idle completion.
- **Subagent Inheritance & Role Confinement:** Subagents inherit active tasks from their parent session via the `parentID` hierarchy. Subagents spawned with read-only roles (`reviewer`, `planner`, `advisor`, `critic`, `explorer`, `scout`, `evaluator`) are hard-confined. File mutations, lifecycle tools, and mutating shell commands are strictly blocked. On OpenCode 2 the confinement is two-layered. `session.hook("context")` deletes the mutating tools (`write`, `edit`, `patch`, `apply_patch`, `shell`, `bash`, `execute`, `todowrite`, `subagent`/`task`, worktree lifecycle tools) from that role's per-request tool snapshot. `execute.before` stays as the backstop for tools supplied outside the snapshot, such as ACP agents and nested Code Mode calls. The pruning is journaled as `session.context` / `read_only_role_tools_pruned`.
- **Handoff Safety:** An idle subagent whose effective todos are inherited from its parent is not auto-continued. Inherited work belongs to the parent and can be handed back normally.
- **Durable Planning Context Discovery:** `guard_next_tasks` prefers a repository-root `TODO.md`. When it is absent, it reads conventional `ROADMAP.md`, `PLAN.md`, `TASKS.md`, `BACKLOG.md`, their `docs/` counterparts, and Markdown files under `docs/plans/`. The tool exposes candidate planning context without selecting, prioritizing, or sequencing tasks. These files never replace OpenCode's native runtime todo state.
- **Subagent Mutation Budget:** Subagent sessions are protected by a mutation safety budget (`maxSubagentMutations` in project config or `WORKFLOW_GUARD_MAX_SUBAGENT_MUTATIONS` env, default 100). The budget terminates runaway edit loops deterministically.
- **Concurrent File Claims:** Direct `edit`, `write`, and `apply_patch` calls claim each canonical target for the tool-call lifetime. A different active session is blocked from racing the same file, including through symlink aliases. Claims are released after the call, with session idle/deletion as stale-claim cleanup when an after hook is missed. Two provable staleness rules reclaim a leaked claim, each audited, and both stay scoped to the contended paths so a long-running command elsewhere keeps its claim. The idle rule releases a claim created before its owner's last recorded idle timestamp, because that call finished before the turn ended. It writes a `stale_claim_takeover` entry. The TTL rule releases a claim older than the effective claim TTL, which covers a deleted session and a server restart where the owner record cannot be read at all. It writes a `claim_ttl_expired` entry with the owner and claim age. The TTL defaults to five minutes, is raised or lowered with `claimTtlMs` in `.opencode/workflow-guard.json`, and `WORKFLOW_GUARD_CLAIM_TTL_MS` wins over project config. A non-positive or unparseable value falls back to the default. Owners still mid-session within the TTL, clients without a session lookup, and failed lookups keep the block (fail-closed). The block names the owner, the claim age, and the reclaim step. `guard_why` stays read-only and still reports the conflict as blocked. A recognized shell writer is refused with the same reason when its target is claimed: redirection, `tee`, `sed -i`, `cp`/`mv`/`ln`, `rm`, `truncate`, `dd of=`, `git apply`, and `git am`. A `mv` source is checked too, because the move removes it. The check resolves a relative target against the tree the segment actually runs in, so a chained `cd` and a symlink alias are judged where the write lands. A shell write never acquires a claim, so it cannot strand one the edit path must later reclaim, and the provably stale rules release before the conflict is reported. Shell writers remain outside the write-observation and stale-write pre-check, and isolated worktrees remain the better choice for substantial parallel mutations.
- **Stale-Write Protection:** A successful `read` records a same-session fingerprint for an existing regular file from five fields. Those fields are canonical path, filesystem identity, size, nanosecond mtime, and SHA-256 content digest. A successful `edit`/`write` also records the resulting bytes, and only when the file actually changed. The session authored those bytes, so iterating on a just-created or just-modified file needs no redundant re-read. Before `edit` or `write` replaces an existing file, that fingerprint must exist and still match. Otherwise the call is blocked and must re-read. New-file creation is allowed without a prior read. Fingerprints are not inherited between parent and subagent sessions, and they are cleared on session idle or deletion. `apply_patch` and shell writers sit deliberately outside this bounded mechanism. An `apply_patch` result still seeds the session observation, but its clobbering itself is not pre-checked. The pre-execution comparison also cannot make external changes between the check and OpenCode's write atomic.
- **Shell-redirect seeding:** An allowed shell command that redirects into a workspace file (`cmd > file`, `cmd >> file`, fd forms) seeds the session's observation of the resulting bytes. It does so in the same change-gated way as direct edits. A file this session just created or rewrote via a shell redirect can therefore be edited without a redundant re-read. Redirects to `/dev/null`, the `/tmp/opencode` scratch directory, or outside the workspace seed nothing. An identical-byte (no-op) redirect does not seed. The not-read block message also suggests coordinating when another session may own the file. Shell writers themselves remain outside the bounded pre-check, so only the observation seeding applies.

### 2. No Pushes to Protected Branches
- `git push ... main` and `git push ... master` are blocked in all shell commands, including direct refs, refspecs (`git push origin HEAD:main`, `git push origin feature/x:main`), deletion refspecs (`git push origin :main`), and forced refspecs (`git push origin +main`).
- Branches configured via `protectedBranches` in `.opencode/workflow-guard.json` receive the same destination-side push protection (`git push origin feature/x:release/prod` is blocked).
- Git global options (`-C`, `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`, `-c`) are parsed before matching, so `git -C /repo push origin main` is gated on `/repo`'s branch.
- Normal pushes and force-pushes to feature branches are allowed.

### 3. PR Changelog, Changesets & Lockfile Synchronization Requirement
- `gh pr create` and `az repos pr create` are blocked unless:
  - The branch diff modifies a `CHANGELOG` file, OR
  - The branch diff adds/modifies a `.changeset/*.md` fragment file (Changesets workflow), OR
  - The PR description (`--body`, `--description`, or `--body-file`/`-F`) contains a release-information section headed `Changelog`, `Changes`, `Release notes`, or `Summary`. Multiline Bash ANSI-C `\n`/`\r` quoting is supported for inline descriptions. Inline descriptions that would render Markdown line breaks as literal `\n`/`\r` text are blocked. The block message directs the author to real newlines or a description file.
- **Lockfile Synchronization Gate:** Whenever package manifests (`package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`) are modified, PR creation is blocked until their corresponding lockfiles are updated. Those lockfiles are `package-lock.json`/`bun.lock`/`pnpm-lock.yaml`/`yarn.lock`, `Cargo.lock`, and `go.sum`. For `package.json` the demand is section-aware. It fires when a section the lockfile records changed. Those sections are `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, `peerDependencies`, `peerDependenciesMeta`, `engines`, `packageManager`, `overrides`, `resolutions`, `workspaces`, `pnpm`, and the project `name` or `version`. Scripts- or metadata-only manifest edits regenerate the lockfile byte-identical and pass without one. `Cargo.toml` and `go.mod` changes conservatively keep demanding their lockfiles.
- When multiple PR prerequisites fail at once, the guard reports all detected preflight failures together so they can be resolved before retrying PR creation.

### 11. Secret-Content Scan
- File payloads and recognized shell file-mutation commands are scanned for common credential material. That material includes AWS keys, private key headers, GitHub tokens, OpenAI and LLM keys, Google API keys, Slack tokens, and explicit env-style assignments.
- Flagged content is blocked before the write with an actionable message. Secret-file reads also resolve existing symlink aliases, and copying/moving/linking a known secret path under another name is blocked.

### 12. Shell Environment Scrub
- Sensitive environment variables are **emptied** in agent shells by the `shell.env` hook. The list covers `AWS_*`, `KUBE*`, `OPENAI*`, `ANTHROPIC*`, `GOOGLE_/GCP_`, `AZURE_`, `SLACK_`, `NPM_`, `DOCKER_`, `KUBECONFIG`, and fixed names like `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `KUBECONFIG`, and `NPM_TOKEN`. GitHub tokens (`GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`) are preserved so `gh` CLI and git operations function without recurring login prompts.
- This prevents the agent from carrying live credentials by default. The user can still grant access through OpenCode's own permission system if a task genuinely needs it.

## Known Limits (Defense in Depth)

These guards match on command strings, file structures, and interpreter payloads (including base64 pipeline decoding and inline eval scans under Policy 18). While inline scripts are decoded and analyzed, compiled binaries or multi-stage external downloads require OS-level sandboxing. This plugin is a **hardened deterrent against forgetful, complacent, or prompt-injected agents**, not an OS kernel sandbox. Pair it with:
- GitHub branch protection/rulesets server-side
- OS-level workspace isolation (containers, read-only mounts)

for hard guarantees.

# Static Policy Posture

Workflow Guard has three enforcement seats. Two of them live inside the plugin:

| Seat | Runs in | Removed by |
|---|---|---|
| `ctx.permission.hook("evaluate")` | the plugin | uninstalling or disabling the plugin |
| `execute.before` | the plugin | uninstalling or disabling the plugin |
| static configuration policies | the host | editing the config that carries them |

Static policies are the only layer a repository cannot lift. A project cannot
grant itself a permission the host denies in global config, because the host
resolves static policy before any plugin hook runs. That is the whole point of
this surface, and it is also why the plugin refuses to install it for you.

## Emit, do not install

```
opencode-workflow-guard policies --print
opencode-workflow-guard policies --print --format 2.0
opencode-workflow-guard policies --print --format next
```

The command writes JSONC to stdout and nothing else. It refuses to run without
`--print`. A plugin that can write the configuration holding its own static
rails has moved those rails back inside the plugin, so the operator places the
block.

The default is `both`, which emits each rule under the key its host reads:

| Format | Envelope | Rule action | Host that reads it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `both` (default) | `experimental.policies` and top-level `policies` | `permission` and `tool.use` | 2.0.x and 2.1.x |
| `2.0` | `experimental.policies` | `permission` | 2.0.x only |
| `next` | top-level `policies` | `tool.use` | 2.1.x only |

The envelopes are not interchangeable, and neither host warns about the one it
does not read. OpenCode 2.0.x evaluates `experimental.policies` with
`action === "permission"` and ignores a top-level `policies` array entirely.
OpenCode 2.1.x evaluates the top-level `policies` array with
`action === "tool.use"` and ignores `experimental.policies`. A single-key block
therefore looks applied on the other host and enforces nothing.

Both hosts read only their own key, so carrying both cannot double-apply a rule
or make them conflict. `--format 2.0` and `--format next` exist for a pinned
host. `both` is the default, because the silent no-op is the failure this
surface exists to prevent.

Schema acceptance is not runtime acceptance. `@opencode/schema` 2.0.10 admits a
top-level `policies` array that the 2.0.15 runtime never reads, so a decode test
grades the block as valid while the host enforces nothing. The envelope table
above is verified by live denial canaries on both hosts, in the acceptance
section below.

## What is emitted

| Rule | Action | Resource | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| protected trunk push | `shell` | `git push * main`, `git push * master`, `git push * HEAD:main`, `git push * HEAD:master` | trunk must stay protected when the plugin is absent |
| live control plane write | `edit` | `*/.config/opencode/*`, `/etc/opencode/*`, `/Library/Application Support/opencode/*` | an agent that can edit the control plane can rewrite its own constraints |
| secret material read | `read` | `*/.ssh/*`, `*id_rsa*` | private keys should never enter a model context |
| external directory widening | `external_directory` | `*` | `external_directory` defaults to allow; denying it is what makes the write boundary a boundary |
| Code Mode surface | `execute` | `*` | removes the nested tool surface where the host asserts the action |

Every emitted rule is a denial. A posture that granted access would be a second,
weaker policy engine in a config file, and the plugin already owns that job.

The control-plane rule starts with `*/` rather than `~/` on purpose: 2.0.x
expands `~` and `$HOME` only for the `permissions` key, not for
`experimental.policies`, so a tilde resource would never match an absolute path.
`*/.config/opencode/*` is version-independent and covers every home directory.

Two of these are judgement calls rather than obvious wins, so drop them
deliberately if they conflict with normal work:

- `external_directory: *` denies every path outside the active project. Cross
  repository reads then require an explicit later `allow` rule. That is the
  strict posture, and it is the one the write-confinement work assumes.
- `execute: *` removes Code Mode. The qualified hosts (2.0.15 and 2.1.3)
  register no `execute` tool and never assert an `execute` permission action,
  so the rule is inert on both and Code Mode stays available. On a host that
  does assert the action, the rule removes a surface whose nested tool calls
  this guard does not evaluate. The plugin's read-only tool pruning and
  `execute.before` remain the coverage today.

## Precedence

Highest authority first:

| Authority | Source |
|---|---|
| 0 | managed preferences and Console policies |
| 2 | `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` |
| 3 | `/etc/opencode` |
| 4 | `~/.config/opencode` |
| 5 | project `opencode.json(c)` |

Within one ruleset the last matching rule wins. Across documents the earlier
authority wins. Two consequences matter when you place the block:

1. Put it in the system or global config (authority 3 or 4), never in a project
   file. A project file is the scope the rules are meant to outrank.
2. If you add broad `allow` rules for local workflows, place these denies after
   them in the same file. A deny that lands earlier is shadowed.

On 2.0.x, the host builds its rule list by reversing the document order and
then taking the last match per resource, so a global document beats a project
document for the same resource. Verified in the 2.0.15 binary
(`opencode.config.policy`).

## Residual risk

Read this before treating the block as a sandbox.

- Policies do not sandbox plugin code. A plugin can still do anything the
  process can do.
- A process that can write the file carrying these rules can remove them. File
  ownership and permissions are the control there, not policy.
- Shell patterns match the whole command string. `cd /tmp && git push origin
  main` does not match `git push * main`, and neither does an exotic refspec
  spelled differently. The static floor covers the direct forms only. This gap
  is covered by a regression test, which asserts the evasion succeeds so the
  limit stays visible.
- A denied provider is blocked on the normal path only. Alternate paths are not
  covered by `provider.use` policies.
- Effect values are `allow` and `deny`. There is no `ask` at this seat, which is
  why the emitted rules deny rather than prompt.

## Acceptance status

**Status: RUN.** The canary installs the emitted block into an isolated project
config and drives a real model turn that calls the denied tool. It is run once
per host.

| Host | Emitted block | Probed rule | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0.15 | `--format 2.0` | `shell:printf*` | `Blocked by configuration policy` |
| 2.1.3 | `--format 2.0` | `shell:printf*` | **executed** (silent no-op) |
| 2.0.15 | `--format next` | `shell:printf*` | **executed** (silent no-op) |
| 2.1.3 | `--format next` | `shell:printf*` | `Blocked by configuration policy` |
| 2.0.15 | default (`both`) | `read:*id_rsa*` | `Blocked by configuration policy` |
| 2.1.3 | default (`both`) | `read:*id_rsa*` | `Blocked by configuration policy` |

The two silent no-ops are the defect this section exists to prevent, and they
are why the default emits both envelopes. A single-key block is not merely
unverified on the other host. It is actively misleading there, because the
config loads and reports no error.

Two limits on the canary, so nobody over-reads it:

- The `write` tool is gated by the `edit` permission action on 2.1.3 but not on
  2.0.15, so a `write` canary would not have proved the `edit` rule on both.
  The `read` rule was chosen for the cross-host proof because both hosts map it
  identically.
- The `execute` invariant stays inert on both qualified hosts, because neither
  registers an `execute` tool. Its canary cannot pass until a host asserts the
  action, and the rule is documented as inert rather than claimed as coverage.

Placing the block in a live control-plane path stays out of scope for an agent:
the tamper policy refuses that write, and that refusal is correct. The canary
uses an isolated project config instead, which exercises the same evaluator.

The emitted resources are also asserted against a replica of the host matcher in
`test/test.mts`, and both envelopes are required to reach the same verdict for
every probed resource.

To run the canary yourself, install the block into `~/.config/opencode`, then
attempt a denied action in a live session and confirm the message names
configuration policy rather than the plugin. Use the default (`both`) envelope
unless you have pinned the host, and check the result on the host you actually
run.

# Testing & Verification Guide

This repository includes both in-memory unit tests and live runtime installation tests.

## Test Commands

### 1. Build & Typecheck
Runs strict TypeScript compilation checks across all source and test files:
```bash
npm run typecheck   # or: npm run build
```

### 2. In-Memory Unit Tests
Runs the unit and adversarial tests covering all guard policies, lifecycle validation, subagent parent-chain resolution, privilege-isolated verification, and path/symlink boundary checks:
```bash
npm test            # runs test.mts with isolated XDG state/data (Node >= 22.18)
```

### 3. OpenCode Runtime & Install Tests
Packs the npm tarball into an isolated project to verify the modular entrypoint resolves. It then copies the server source into an isolated `.opencode/workflow-guard-source/` directory. That source's `WorkflowGuard` plugin function is exposed through an explicitly registered `.opencode/plugins/` adapter. A provider-free config probe verifies OpenCode resolves that local plugin before the opt-in model-driven `opencode run` probes exercise its hooks:
```bash
npm run test:install # package install + provider-free OpenCode loader check
WORKFLOW_GUARD_LIVE_E2E=1 npm run test:install # also run model-driven policy probes with OpenCode's most recently selected model
```
Package and loader checks remain deterministic. Live probes explicitly select the first entry in OpenCode's persisted recent-model state (`${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/opencode/model.json`). They never silently inherit the configured default model. Set `WORKFLOW_GUARD_LIVE_MODEL=provider/model` to override that selection. Provider credentials still come from the normal OpenCode environment. A provider may reject a live prompt before guard behavior can run. That happens when credits, rate limits, capacity, overload, or an unresolvable model make the provider unavailable. Such a case is reported as unavailable rather than as a guard failure. The classifier matches the host's literal `Model unavailable:` error line rather than the bare phrase, so model prose cannot mask a real guard regression. Other live-runtime failures still fail the suite.

The suite needs a temp directory with room for a full `node_modules` copy. On a host whose `os.tmpdir()` is a small tmpfs, a nearly full one fails `npm pack` and `npm install` with `Unknown system error -122` (`EDQUOT`). Point `TMPDIR` at a filesystem-backed directory in that case, for example `TMPDIR=/var/tmp npm run test:install`. The harness stops every managed service it starts before removing its temporary project, so a run no longer leaves a detached server writing into the directory it is deleting.

### 4. Full Verification Suite
Runs typecheck, unit tests, and live runtime installation tests in sequence:
```bash
npm run test:all
```

# Troubleshooting Guide

Common issues, root causes, and solutions when using `opencode-workflow-guard`.

---

### 1. `plugin config hook failed` / `Unexpected server error` on startup

- **Symptoms:** OpenCode crashes or reports `Unexpected server error` when starting a session, with logs showing `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating '...event')`.
- **Root Cause:** OpenCode 1.18+'s legacy loader treats *every exported function* in a plugin module as a separate plugin instance. A plugin that exports helper functions (like `guardToolCall` or `setWorkspaceRoot`) alongside a default function therefore registers those helpers as plugins too. OpenCode calls them as plugins, pushes `undefined` into the hook registry, and crashes event dispatch on `session.created`.
- **Solution:** Ensure `src/workflow-guard.ts` uses the V1 `PluginModule` export format (`export default { id: "workflow-guard", server: WorkflowGuard } satisfies PluginModule`). File plugins require an explicit `id` string.

---

### 2. Edits Blocked: `Blocked: no active todo item`

- **Symptoms:** The agent attempts an edit (`edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`) and receives a block message directing it to create a task list.
- **Root Cause:** Policy 1 blocks file-editing tools while the session's **effective** todo list is known and contains no task with status `pending` or `in_progress`. On OpenCode 1.x that list is the native todo state (`GET /session/:id/todo`). Before 2.1.0, OpenCode 2.x has no todo endpoint and no builtin `todowrite`. The list is then reconstructed from the newest applied `todowrite` tool call in the session history, which some ACP agents supply. A list counts as empty only when a `todowrite` part actually exists. When the session has no `todowrite` capability at all, the gate fails open rather than blocking every edit forever.
- **Solution:** The agent must call `todowrite` first. Once all tasks are marked `completed` or `cancelled`, edits block again until a new breakdown is created for subsequent work. If an agent on OpenCode 2.x is blocked here despite having no todo tool available, that is a bug. Report it rather than working around it through shell writes.

---

### 3. Multiple tasks are `in_progress`

- **Symptoms:** A task list contains multiple `in_progress` items during parallel work.
- **Root Cause:** This is supported. Policy 1 permits multiple tasks to be `in_progress` so independent work and subagents can proceed concurrently.
- **Solution:** No correction is required. Keep each active item in every replacement list until it is explicitly marked `completed` or `cancelled`.

---

### 4. `Blocked todowrite: active task '...' was removed`

- **Symptoms:** `todowrite` is blocked after an active item disappears from the submitted list.
- **Root Cause:** Each `todowrite` call replaces the complete list. Policy 1 therefore requires active tasks to be explicitly completed or cancelled rather than silently omitted. Independent items may otherwise be completed out of order.
- **Solution:** Keep the task in the list and mark it `completed` or `cancelled` before removing it in a later request.

---

### 5. Edits Blocked: `Blocked: the workspace is on a protected branch (main/master)`

- **Symptoms:** Direct edits or git commit/merge commands are rejected.
- **Root Cause:** Policy 7 requires all code modifications to happen on a feature branch.
- **Solution:** Switch to a feature branch (`git switch -c feat/my-feature`) before making changes.

A checkout that is only behind its remote is not blocked. `git merge --ff-only <upstream>`, `git rebase <upstream>`, and `git pull --ff-only` are allowed on the protected branch when the ref is the branch's tracked upstream or the remote default, and `HEAD` is already an ancestor of it. That adds no commit and rewrites none, so a stale primary checkout can sync without a feature branch. `git merge` without `--ff-only`, a bare `git pull`, a local branch target, a different remote branch, a named remote and branch, and a branch with its own commits stay blocked. On a host where `pull.rebase` is set, run `git -c pull.rebase=false pull --ff-only`; the guard accepts that form.

The cleanup a merged PR requires is also allowed on the protected branch. `git branch -d <branch>` and `git branch --delete <branch>` pass, because git itself refuses them unless the branch is fully merged. A remote branch that is already merged can be deleted with `git push origin --delete <branch>` or `git push origin :<branch>`. A forced deletion, `git branch -D`, a protected branch name, an unmerged branch, and the options that delete more than the named branches (`--prune`, `--mirror`) stay blocked.

---

### 6. Edits Blocked: `Blocked: file path '...' escapes workspace root`

- **Symptoms:** Edits targeting files with `../` or external absolute paths are rejected.
- **Root Cause:** Policy 8 prevents directory traversal outside the workspace root.
- **Solution:** Ensure all target file paths resolve within the project directory.

---

### 7. Subagents Cannot Edit Files

- **Symptoms:** A subagent spawned via `task` fails to edit files.
- **Root Cause:** OpenCode disables `todowrite` for subagents by default.
- **Solution:** The guard automatically walks up the `parentID` session hierarchy so subagents inherit the parent session's active tasks. Ensure the parent session has active tasks before a subagent attempts guarded mutations.

---

### 8. Destructive Commands Blocked (`kubectl`, `terraform`, `psql`, etc.)

- **Symptoms:** A CLI command is rejected with a live-system mutation warning.
- **Root Cause:** Policy 4 blocks destructive cloud, database, and infrastructure operations.
- **Solution:** To intentionally run a live command, set `WORKFLOW_GUARD_ALLOW_LIVE=1` in the environment before launching OpenCode. There is no in-command override. An agent cannot grant this permission to itself.

---

### 9. TUI plugin is missing or remains on an older release

- **Symptoms:** Workflow Guard does not appear in the TUI, or npm reports a newer Workflow Guard release while OpenCode still runs an older one.
- **Root Cause:** OpenCode caches npm plugins. A bare package name is resolved as `@latest`, but an already-populated package cache can continue using the version that originally populated that cache key. Running `npm update` in `~/.config/opencode` does not update this OpenCode-managed plugin installation.
- **Solution:** Use OpenCode's documented plugin installer with the explicit version you want. `--force` replaces the configured plugin version, and the explicit version gives OpenCode a new package-cache key:

```bash
VERSION=$(npm view opencode-workflow-guard version)
opencode plugin "opencode-workflow-guard@$VERSION" --global --force
```

OpenCode documents `opencode plugin <module>` as installing a plugin and updating its config, with `--global` for global config and `--force` to replace an existing plugin version: https://opencode.ai/docs/cli/#plugin. Its plugin documentation also describes npm plugins as OpenCode-managed, cached installations: https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/#how-plugins-are-installed.

After the command reports `Detected server + tui targets`, confirm it reports replacements/additions for both the OpenCode and TUI config files, then restart OpenCode. Manual cache deletion should not be necessary.

---

### 10. TUI companion crashes with `Keymap.Provider is missing` (OpenCode V2)

- **Symptoms:** On opencode v2, the TUI companion plugin fails during setup with `Keymap.Provider is missing` and does not load.
- **Root Cause:** `ctx.keymap.layer` resolves a Solid context (`useContext(KeymapContext)`), so it only works inside the TUI's `Keymap.Provider` render tree. The API documents layers as "owned by the calling component". Plugin `setup()` runs as a plain async call outside that tree, so registering a layer there always throws.
- **Solution:** Fixed in 1.13.2. The layer is registered from an `app`-slot claim (`ctx.ui.slot({ append: "app", render: () => { ...; return null } })`). Slot renders execute in a reactive scope under the provider, and the same session-panel pattern applies to any plugin API that requires component ownership. If you maintain a TUI plugin that registers keymap layers, commands, or reactive state, register them from a slot render or a rendered component. Never register them from `setup()`.

---

### 11. Reading tool parts from V2 sessions (integrators)

- **Symptoms:** Code that parses recorded tool calls finds no tool name on OpenCode V2. It may also see tool names that do not exist in OpenCode's builtin tool list. The affected sources are message parts, the `part` DB table, and `session.message.content.updated` events.
- **Root Cause:** Two independent things:
  1. V2 message parts record the tool name in the `tool` field, where V1 used `name`. Code reading `part.name` silently gets `undefined` on V2.
  2. V2's builtin tool registry contains only `read`, `glob`, `grep`, `edit`, `write`, `patch`, `shell`, `webfetch`, `websearch`, `question`, `skill`, `subagent`, and `execute`. There is no builtin `todowrite`, which is the V1 name, and the V1 `task` subagent tool was renamed to `subagent`. `todowrite` and `bash` tool parts observed in V2 sessions come from ACP agents, for example pi, that supply their own tools. Those tools are not in the server-side registry and cannot be reached by `ctx.tool.transform`.
- **Solution:** Read the tool name as `part.tool ?? part.name` and treat tool-part names as agent-reported, not as the builtin registry. `ToolEditor.update` ignores missing IDs, so enriching a tool that does not exist is a harmless no-op.

---

### 12. Review recorded with `record_review`, but `pr create` is still blocked

- **Symptoms:** `record_review` returned "Review recorded as APPROVED" and `guard_status` showed a fresh `lastReview`, yet `pr create` was blocked with "Passing secondary review approval is required". A re-call of `record_review` may return success while `guard_status` still shows no fresh review.
- **Root Cause (fixed by content binding):** The PR preflight previously also required the review's target session to equal the PR-creating session's ID. `record_review` records from a secondary session, binding the verdict to its parent or its own directory. Sessions can move between directories mid-flight (`session_move`), and subagents spawn from other roots. A review recorded against a linked git worktree could therefore never satisfy a PR created from another session there. Mutation invalidation also erased the whole review record on any mutation, including unrelated untracked-file cleanup.
- **Binding rule:** A recorded approval satisfies the preflight when its binding matches the tree the PR publishes. The binding covers the repository, the commit hash, and the tracked-content worktree fingerprint. Review freshness is scoped to tracked content. Deleting an untracked scratch file does not invalidate it, and a tracked edit or new commit does. When the tracked fingerprint is unchanged but HEAD moved, the preflight names the commit drift specifically. That case arises when a review is recorded with changes already staged and then committed. The remedy is the same either way: record the review at the commit that will ship.
- **Commit before you review:** both evidence gates bind to the HEAD commit hash, so a commit after verification or after the review invalidates that evidence. Finish every tracked change first, then verify, then record the review, then open the PR. Any other order costs a re-run.
- **Diagnosis:** `guard_audit` records the binding key on every `record_review.verdict` entry. The key covers workspace, commit hash, fingerprint prefix, recorder session, and `recorderRole`. It also records a `pr-preflight.review-binding` entry when a PR preflight accepts a review. A verdict that cannot bind at all is rejected loudly with the reason instead of returning a success string. That case is a directory that is not a git repository.
- **Strict recorder mode rejects the approval:** Projects with `requireSubagentReview: true` (or `WORKFLOW_GUARD_REQUIRE_SUBAGENT_REVIEW=1`) reject `record_review` approval verdicts recorded by the root session. The message reads "this project requires approvals to be recorded from a subagent session", and the `guard_audit` entry carries reason `subagent_recorder_required`. Record the verdict from a subagent session (one with a parent session) instead, or disable the requirement in project config. Changes-requested verdicts remain relayable from any session. The knob is enforced when verdicts are recorded. An approval recorded by the root session before the requirement was enabled still satisfies the PR preflight until its content binding goes stale. That includes durable review-cache evidence recovered after a restart. Re-run the secondary review after adopting the knob to re-bind it.
- **Worktree creation failure leaving a branch behind:** `guard_worktree_create` failures previously surfaced only git's stderr. That output is often just checkout progress, and the failure could leave a half-created branch. Failures now report git's exit status, and the created branch is rolled back. Pre-existing branches are preserved. Stale worktree admin entries are pruned only for the newly-created path. A live registered worktree whose sanitized name collides with the requested branch is left fully intact, because rollback never removes pre-existing worktrees. Large checkouts that exceed the 15s timeout can raise it with `WORKFLOW_GUARD_WORKTREE_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- **Edit blocked by a file claim though no other session is working:** A missed `session.idle` release, a deleted session, or a server restart can leave a finished session's direct-edit claim behind. Two provable staleness rules reclaim it, each audited. A claim created before its owner's last recorded idle timestamp is provably stale and is released with a `stale_claim_takeover` entry in `guard_audit`. A claim older than the effective TTL is released even when the owner record cannot be read, with a `claim_ttl_expired` entry that names the owner and claim age. The TTL defaults to five minutes. Raise or lower it with `claimTtlMs` in `.opencode/workflow-guard.json`, or `WORKFLOW_GUARD_CLAIM_TTL_MS` (the environment wins). A non-positive or unparseable value falls back to the default. The block message names the owner, the claim age, and the reclaim step. Owners still mid-turn within the TTL keep their claim. The takeover fails closed without an SDK session lookup, and when the lookup fails. `guard_why` remains read-only and still reports the conflict.
- **You updated the plugin but the old version still loads:** A configured bare package name is resolved through Node's parent-directory lookup from OpenCode's configuration location. A copy in any parent `node_modules` (a pnpm-managed home directory or a manual install) shadows OpenCode's own plugin cache and a global `npm install -g`. OpenCode's own update check can then fail with only a server-log record (`NpmInstallFailedError`). Verify what actually loaded with `guard_status` (the `pluginVersion` field), the startup app-log line (`Workflow Guard v<version> plugin initialized ...`), or the server log's `loading plugin ... entrypoint=file:///...` record. Then update the resolved copy in place (for a pnpm-managed home directory: `cd ~ && pnpm add opencode-workflow-guard@<version>`). Run `opencode service restart`, because the plugin loads in the background service and restarting only the TUI does not reload it.
- **A benign-looking command with a shell variable is blocked as "outside the workspace":** A mutation or redirect target that contains an unresolvable `$VARIABLE` reference is indeterminate without executing shell semantics. Examples are `mkdir -p $D/sub`, `cp a.txt "$D/b.txt"`, and `> $CACHE/out.txt`. The boundary fails closed on indeterminate destinations. The block message names this cause: "contains an unresolvable variable reference … use a literal workspace-relative path". Deterministically expandable forms (`~`, `$HOME`) and literal paths inside the workspace are unaffected. Reads, including cache-path reads, are not gated. Replace the variable with a literal workspace-relative path in the command. Alternatively, assign it inside a script file within the workspace that the boundary has already validated. Resolving the variable would need shell execution, which the boundary deliberately avoids.
- **A scratch write to `/tmp/opencode` is blocked:** A write there is allowed for a real session when the target's canonical location stays inside that exact directory. The root must be a real directory, not a symlink. A symlink inside it that leaves the directory is refused, and so is a sibling path that merely shares the prefix or a `..` traversal out of it. A write with no session id is also blocked. Use a real path under `/tmp/opencode` or an untracked file inside the workspace, for example `.tmp-notes.md`. The allowance is a file-mutation allowance only, and the boundary has no override for anything outside it.
- **A reviewer agent cannot call `record_review`:** The guard registers `record_review` for every session, independent of `requireReview`. A host with a per-agent permission list can still withhold the call, and a reviewer agent that starts from a deny-all list (`action: "*"`, `resource: "*"`, `effect: deny`) does exactly that. The guard cannot inject the tool past host permissions, so grant it in that agent's own frontmatter with an explicit allow rule for `record_review`, or relay the verdict through a session that already has the tool. `guard_status` reporting the review gate as required proves nothing about the reviewer's toolset. This is a permission grant in the agent definition, not a guard policy change.

# RSI experiment ledger

Structured, create-only record of every base-loop attempt, accepted or
rejected. One record per iteration; append only. Never edit or delete a prior
record: a negative result is data, not clutter.

## Schema (one block per iteration)

```text
n · date (UTC) · hypothesis (falsifiable) · trace evidence · code change ·
commit SHA + git tree · artifact name + checksum · exact command/config ·
test results · eval job path · score · gains · losses · exceptions ·
token/cost/duration · interpretation · keep/revert · next hypothesis
```

Schema v2 adds two fields, required on every new record:

```text
selection score (n items) · held-out score (n items, never used for selection)
· prev-chain: sha256:<hex of the preceding record block>
```

`selection score` is the score on the items the loop selected against.
`held-out score` is the score on a disjoint item set never used for
selection. Report both (winner's curse). `prev-chain` links each record to
the sha256 of the prior record block so the create-only rule is
tamper-evident (hash-chained admission).

## Rules

- Append only. One block per iteration. No rewrites, renumbering, or deletes.
- Report `selection score` and `held-out score` side by side; a `keep`
  requires a non-empty `held-out score`. Held-out items are never reused for
  selection.
- `prev-chain` is the sha256 of the preceding record block.
- Record failures with the same care as successes; an empty failures column
  is a smell, not a clean run.
- Name idiosyncratic infrastructure/verifier constraints explicitly, so a
  later reader does not re-derive them.
- Every `keep` cites the eval run that justified it; every `revert` keeps the
  failure evidence and the next hypothesis.
- A record is written by the base loop, not a subagent.

# RSI loop playbook

The operating manual for the `/rsi-loop` and `/rsi-campaign` commands, and the
repo-local grounding those commands read first. The top half is the scaffold
template; the anchors at the bottom are this repository's own pain points,
verifier, and metric.

## Before the first iteration

The loop depends on three artifacts in this repo. Create any missing one from
`~/.config/opencode/templates/rsi/` before running an iteration:

- `docs/agents/rsi-loop-playbook.md` — this file.
- `docs/agents/ledger.md` — the create-only experiment ledger.
- `docs/agents/lessons.md` and `docs/agents/lessons/` — the lesson memory.

## The base loop

One iteration maps to one branch and one PR:

1. **PROPOSE** — pick one minimal candidate change. Read the actual code first;
   cite the files you read in the proposal.
2. **PREDICT** — before editing, register a falsifiable claim: expected effect
   on the metric, how it will be verified, and at-risk regressions.
3. **IMPLEMENT** — delegate mechanical work to an `executor` subagent with a
   full spec (inputs, constraints, acceptance command). Keep the diff minimal.
   Start on the cheap tier; escalate only on an observable trigger.
4. **EVALUATE** — run the external verifier only; self-review is not evidence.
   Change one causal axis per iteration.
5. **SELECT** — regularize selection: anneal the edit budget, screen proposals
   for benchmark-specific trickery, prune stale or too-small edits, and advance
   the incumbent only on a minimum effect size. Delegate a fresh-eyes check to
   a `reviewer` subagent. Archive rejected attempts with their failure evidence.
6. **REMEMBER** — write one lesson file under `docs/agents/lessons/`, and append
   one structured record to `docs/agents/ledger.md`. Write it either way; a
   negative result is data.

## Hard rules

- Never edit tests, the verifier, baselines, or run logs to make a change pass.
- Live settings changes go through a sanctioned installer, never a direct edit.
- A negative result is a valid result: log it and stop.

## Multi-iteration campaigns

`/rsi-loop` runs one iteration. `/rsi-campaign` runs a bounded batch (3-5
iterations) in one session with explicit stop brakes and subagent fan-out: it
builds a diversity-tagged candidate set before iterating, enforces no-gain and
same-type stop brakes, and isolates overlapping edits in git worktrees. Each
iteration still maps to one branch and one PR.

## Anchors for this repository

- **verifier** — `npm run typecheck && npm test` in the repository root. Both
  are deterministic: strict TypeScript compilation, then the in-memory
  adversarial harness in `test/test.mts`. `npm run test:install` is the heavier
  package and loader check, reserved for a change that touches the entrypoint.
- **metric** — false-positive policy blocks. The counterfactual is a command an
  agent legitimately issues, or a legitimate lifecycle update, that a policy
  refuses. The observable proxy is the block count per policy code in the audit
  journal (`~/.local/state/opencode/workflow-guard/workflow-guard.jsonl`,
  `decision: "block"`), paired with a regression case that fails before the fix
  and passes after it. A fix that lowers the block count while removing a real
  detection is a loss, not a gain, so every candidate ships both directions:
  the now-allowed false positive, and a still-blocked true positive.
- **noise floor** — the journal accumulates across sessions and machines, so a
  raw count is not comparable between runs. Every iteration therefore scores
  against a frozen snapshot of the journal and a frozen subset of commands
  quoted in its own block-reason strings, not against a live count.
- **frozen ruler** — the audit journal is read-only evidence. No iteration
  edits, truncates, or regenerates it, and no iteration edits `test/test.mts`
  assertions to make a case pass. The ruler is the historical journal plus the
  policy code at `origin/main`.
- **spirit** — this plugin is a defence-in-depth deterrent against forgetful or
  prompt-injected agents, not a sandbox. A candidate that removes a detection
  class instead of a false positive is rejected, even when the suite stays
  green.

# LL-013 — A lexical workspace-prefix check must not preempt canonical resolution; decide "outside" only when both lexical and canonical resolution are outside

- **Evidence:** Device audit (`~/.local/state/opencode/workflow-guard/workflow-guard.jsonl`), `workspace_escape` 2026-09-27T05:08:31Z: a write to `/home/hunter/.local/share/opencode/worktrees/azure-container-jobs-remote-sandbox/feat-p12-cache-metering-fields/src/integrations/acp-runtime.ts` was blocked against a workspace root under `/var/home/hunter/...` although the host has `/home -> var/home` (verified: `readlink -f /home/hunter` = `/var/home/hunter`), so the target canonicalizes inside the root. Root cause: `isPathOutsideWorkspace` (`src/policies/boundary.ts`) returned `true` on the lexical prefix check before the realpath/nearest-existing-ancestor canonicalization ran. The alias also leaked into tooling: `guard_worktree_create` returned worktree paths spelled `/home/hunter/...`, and an executor session that tried to edit via `/home/...` spellings hit this exact block.
- **Fix:** the lexical verdict is retained and the existing realpath/ancestor canonicalization now runs regardless; the function returns outside only when the lexical resolution is outside AND the canonical resolution is not inside; indeterminate canonicalization keeps the lexical verdict (fail closed). Lexically-inside paths keep the pre-existing canonical check that catches symlinks inside the workspace pointing outside. Four machine-independent regression checks (alias new-file allowed, alias existing-file allowed, escaping symlink existing+new target still blocked); `npm test` 1099 passed, 0 failed.
- **Lesson:** when a boundary check compares paths, the lexical and canonical answers must agree before blocking: block only when both say outside, and let indeterminate canonicalization fail closed to the lexical verdict. Also treat symlink-aliased path spellings in your own tool output (worktree paths, guard messages) as a distribution channel for the alias into downstream sessions.

Review: APPROVE (5 axes). P3 follow-up recorded: a dangling escape symlink inside the workspace (target does not exist) evades the ancestor walk and the OS create lands outside — pre-existing, to be fixed separately.

# LL-009 — Branch-creation staleness classification must skip shell redirection tokens; `&`-segment splitting leaves bare fd operators behind

- **Evidence:** Device audit (`~/.local/state/opencode/workflow-guard/workflow-guard.jsonl`) recorded three `branch_base_behind` blocks on 2026-09-27 whose "explicit start point" was a redirection token: `the explicit start point '2>' could not be resolved as a commit ... fail closed` (04:29:29Z, 04:29:32Z, 06:15:00Z). Root cause: `branchCreationStartPoint` (`src/policies/git.ts`) had no redirection model, and `splitShellSegments` (`src/lib/shell.ts`) splits unquoted `&`, so `git switch -c feat/x 2>&1` reached the parser as a segment ending in bare `2>`, which was classified as the start point and failed closed even when HEAD was fresh.
- **Fix:** `BRANCH_REDIRECTION_OPERATORS` (separated operators, target word skipped with them) plus `BRANCH_REDIRECTION_ATTACHED_RE` (attached forms `2>/dev/null`, `2>&1`, `&>/dev/null`) in `src/policies/git.ts`; valid refs cannot contain `<`/`>`, so no real start point can be mistaken for a redirection. All fail-closed fallbacks (quotes, `$vars`, unknown flags) unchanged per LL-002.
- **Verification:** 8 regression checks in `test/test.mts` Policy 20 block (stale-branch redirect case still blocks with the reason naming the stale branch and not `'2>'`; five fresh-branch redirect forms allowed; stale-SHA start point behind a redirect still blocks as stale; `$WG_REF` still fails closed). `npm run typecheck` green, `npm test` = 1095 passed, 0 failed. First executor run failed its own `2> /dev/null` case (fd-prefixed separated operator), which forced extending the separated-operator match to fd-prefixed forms — the spec's operator set alone was insufficient.
- **Lesson:** When a classifier extracts operands from a shell fragment that passes through segment splitting, enumerate the redirection grammar (fd-prefixed separated operators, attached operator+target, fd duplication) in the same iteration as the classifier change — a partial operator set fails its own adversarial case. Segment splitting at `&` guarantees `n>&m` arrives as a trailing bare `n>` token, so "operator at end of tokens with no following target" is the shape most likely to be missed.

# LL-011 — Verify config plumbing with a fail-closed sentinel: raw passthrough config fields prove the file was read, resolved fields can be satisfied by env inheritance

- **Evidence:** The e2e harness (`test/test-e2e.mts`) never verified that project configuration (`.opencode/workflow-guard.json[c]`, candidates at `src/lib/project-config.ts:65-72`) reaches the real OpenCode runtime: `guard_status` echoes resolved config (`src/lib/custom-tools.ts:279`) but the harness only asserted `workspaceRoot`, so a silent config-loading failure (wrong path, swallowed parse error — `loadProjectConfig` returns `{}` on any parse failure, `src/lib/project-config.ts:111-118`) would degrade to defaults invisibly. The fix seeds sentinel values (`protectedBranches: ["e2e-config-probe-branch"]`, `requireReview: false`) into the isolated testDir and asserts `guard_status` reports them: `npm run test:install` went 25 passed/0 failed → 26 passed/0 failed, `npm run typecheck` green; fresh-eyes reviewer approved with P3 notes only (verdict recorded via `record_review`, bound to commit `921f895`).
- **Lesson:** A config-loading regression is silent by construction — the loader's failure mode IS "fall back to defaults" — so e2e proof must assert a value that only the file can produce: prefer a raw passthrough field with a sentinel that exists nowhere in source (here `protectedBranches`, a `cfg.protectedBranches ?? ["main","master"]` passthrough in `src/lib/custom-tools.ts:241,279`), because resolved fields can be satisfied by other inputs (the reviewer found `requireReview: false` is also reachable via an inherited `WORKFLOW_GUARD_REQUIRE_REVIEW` env var, `src/lib/state.ts:395-396`, so it corroborates but cannot carry the proof), and choose sentinel values that are behaviorally inert for the rest of the harness so the coverage gain cannot perturb the tests it sits inside. The executor delegation for this edit failed on an unrelated harness defect (a freshly spawned subagent session resolved its workspace root to the operator's dotfiles repo, and `session_move` did not re-root the guard's boundary check) — the parent session applied the spec-exact edit itself; spawn-context workspace binding for subagents in worktrees deserves its own investigation.

# LL-010 — Policy-scanner fixtures are unwritable from inside a guarded session by design; redesign the probe around benign inputs that hit the same deterministic policy paths instead of obfuscating or weakening the scanner

- **Evidence:** Extending the provider-free e2e harness (`test/test-e2e.mts`) beyond its single real-runtime policy probe (`guard_why` simulate of a protected-branch push asserted at the pre-change line 359, executed on the V1 hook path line 238 / V2 registered-tool path line 223): the executor subagent tried to write a kubectl destructive-delete fixture string into the test file — intended purely as simulate-only input to `guard_why`, never executed — and the guard's edit-content scanner blocked the write with `destructive/live_mutation_payload` ("Script files are not a way to smuggle destructive commands past the shell guard"). The scanner intentionally does not distinguish simulation fixtures from real payloads, and no in-session override exists (`WORKFLOW_GUARD_ALLOW_LIVE` is honored only when set before OpenCode starts; the in-command `# allow-live` escape was deliberately removed). The executor refused to obfuscate the string (correct), and the scanner even blocked a `git grep` whose pattern merely contained an interactive-editor fixture name (`shell-safety/interactive_tty`), confirming classifier-triggering text is classified wherever it appears.
- **Accepted change (test-only, no src/ changes):** the headless adapter now probes four deterministic policy families through the real OpenCode-loaded plugin's `guard_why` on both V1 and V2 paths with inputs that trigger the classifiers without literal live-destructive strings: read `.env` → `secrets/secret_read`; `cat .env` → `secrets/secret_read` (shell path); write `../outside_escaped.txt` → `boundary/workspace_escape`; `vim notes.txt` → `shell-safety/interactive_tty`. Previously CI never exercised those families in the real runtime (only via opt-in model-driven probes requiring a provider).
- **Verification:** `npm run test:install` 21 passed/0 failed (baseline, pre-change) → 25 passed/0 failed with the change; reproduced a second time on a different base after a concurrent fleet agent's branch switch replaced this worktree's HEAD mid-iteration and wiped the first (uncommitted) application; `npm run typecheck` green. Fresh-eyes reviewer approved across the 5 rubric axes with only P3 notes (probe-map duplication between the V1/V2 runners; missing-tool failure mode changed, not weakened — every new check also asserts `status === "blocked"`); verdict recorded via `record_review`.
- **Lesson:** When extending harness files in a repo whose guard scans edit content, pick probe inputs that trigger the policy classifier without embedding live destructive command strings (secret reads, workspace escapes, interactive TUI apps), dispatch one `guard_why` simulate call per policy family for real-runtime policy-dispatch coverage without a model provider — and treat "fixture unwritable" as a probe-redesign signal, never an invitation to obfuscate or to weaken the scanner. Uncommitted accepted work in a shared multi-agent checkout does not survive another agent's branch switch: commit the verified artifact immediately, scoped to its own files.

# LL-012 — Assert conditional registration surfaces exhaustively, and scrub env overrides that would satisfy a config-gated proof without the config file

- **Evidence:** The e2e harness asserted only 2 of the 18 custom tool ids in the real runtime (`guard_status`, `guard_why` at the pre-change line ~406); the other 16 register inside three conditional spread groups in `src/lib/custom-tools.ts` (`guard_recovery_restore` gated on `isRecoveryCheckpointsEnabled` :148-149, `project_memory_*` on `isProjectMemoryEnabled` :170-197, `learning_*` on `isLearningEnabled` :199-233), so a real-runtime failure of one gate's enablement chain would silently drop tools with no harness signal. The fix extends the sentinel config with `learning: true` and `recoveryCheckpoints: true` and asserts all 18 ids against the `ctx.tool.list()` surface (V2-gated, since only the V2 runner writes the tools list): `npm run test:install` 26 passed/0 failed → 27 passed/0 failed, `npm run typecheck` green; fresh-eyes reviewer verified the 18-id list matches source id-for-id and approved (verdict recorded via `record_review`, bound to commits `adced74` + `1cc8207`).
- **Lesson:** When a harness asserts a registered surface, enumerate it exhaustively and make each enabling input load-bearing: a subset assertion (2 of 18) cannot see a silently missing conditional group, and an env-overridable gate means an inherited variable (here `WORKFLOW_GUARD_LEARNING=1`, `src/lib/state.ts:446-448`, spread into the harness `runtimeEnv`) can satisfy the assertion even if the config file stops being read — scrub the override from the runtime environment exactly like the harness already scrubs `OPENCODE_*`, or the config leg of the proof is decorative. # LL-016 — A false-positive matcher is usually a matcher that disagrees with a tested sibling; align the two instead of adding a rule

- **Evidence:** `/rsi-campaign` on `opencode-workflow-guard`, 3 iterations, ledger n=3/4/5, PRs #226/#228/#229. Every accepted fix landed on a question that a sibling matcher in the same policy core already answered, and every rejected candidate would have added a rule instead. Telemetry: 45 block codes over 7458 journal records; the two `interactive_tty` blocks were both `sudo`-as-grep-pattern, and the same false positive blocked two live commands during the iteration that fixed it.

| Iteration | Broken matcher | Tested sibling that already decided it | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| n=3 | exact-text todo identity rejected a reworded active task | the annotated-normalized lifecycle key (`src/policies/todo.ts:326-357`) | carry the task window across a token-superset refinement |
| n=4 | legacy tamper mode matched every operand of `cp`/`ln`/`install` | fact mode judged the mutation target (`liveControlPlanePaths`) and allowed a guarded source | judge copy-like verbs by destination; `mv` keeps the broad match |
| n=5 | interactive-TTY patterns matched the raw command text | monitors and pagers already matched at command position | read the command word per segment; `sudo` comes from the unwrapper |

- **Fix:** each iteration aligned the broken matcher with its sibling and shipped both directions. The control run restores the base source file alone, never the tests: n=3 makes 8 of the new checks fail against `origin/main`'s sources; n=4 makes 8 fail against `origin/main`'s `tamper.ts` (6 allowances, 2 pre-existing fd-split destinations); n=5 makes 7 fail against the base `shell-safety.ts`. Suite at each iteration tip: 1756 (#226), 1784 (#228), 1809 (#229), each with 0 failed. The two screening rejections (unverified line numbers; no decision change) were the candidates with no sibling to align with.

- **Lesson:** name the sibling before naming the fix. If the same question already has a tested answer in the policy core, the preregistration cites it, the diff inverts the pinned false positive, and the held-out set proves the opposite direction still blocks. If no sibling exists, the candidate needs a design discussion rather than an iteration. A control that restores the base source and leaves the new tests in place is what makes the gain attributable to the alignment alone.

# Title Settle Default Design

## Context

Workflow Guard can automatically continue a root session that still owns unfinished todos. That synthetic continuation can race OpenCode's asynchronous native session-title generation. The existing `titleSettleWorkaround` behavior avoids the race by briefly waiting for native title generation, but it currently requires explicit opt-in even though Workflow Guard's continuation behavior creates the need for the workaround.

## Decision

Enable the title-settle behavior by default. A missing `titleSettleWorkaround` setting means enabled; `titleSettleWorkaround: false` remains an explicit project-level opt-out.

The server and TUI must expose the same effective semantics. The project-options menu therefore renders Title settle workaround as On when the setting is absent, and selecting it persists `false`. Selecting it again persists `true`.

No configuration migration is required. Existing projects that do not mention the setting acquire the safer default automatically, while projects already configured with `false` retain their behavior.

## Scope

- Change effective server behavior from `=== true` to enabled unless explicitly false.
- Change the TUI project-option reader to report the same enabled-by-default value.
- Preserve all existing bounded-wait, ownership, title, provider, and model behavior.
- Update installation and policy documentation to describe the default and opt-out.
- Update regression coverage for default-enabled behavior and explicit-false opt-out.

## Verification

Regression tests must prove that an unconfigured project uses title settling, explicit `false` bypasses title settling, and the TUI reports/toggles the same effective state. The repository typecheck, unit harness, and packaged-install test must remain green.
